intro: San Francisco spent the week proving it can protect people, and admitting it mostly does not until forced. A West Portal redesign cut collisions 60 percent, but only after a crash killed a family of four. In the same edition, a decade-old rape-kit reporting mandate turned out never to have been followed, the city's earthquake sirens stayed dark into their sixth year, and private donors fast-tracked $6 million for police surveillance the public never budgeted. Money and urgency moved quickly toward watching, slowly toward the safeguards the city already promised.
ai_disclosure: This digest is composed with AI assistance from the week's published Brief items, then reviewed and edited by Eric before publish. AI does not write the news. Original reporting is always linked, always credited.

top_stories.source_headline: After a family was killed at a West Portal bus stop, the street was redesigned. Did it work?
top_stories.one_line: SFMTA data showed collisions fell 60 percent around West Portal after the redesign that followed the 2024 crash that killed a family of four, with serious injuries down from 6.7 to 2.7 a year.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: The city got rare, measured proof that its quick-build safety fixes work, and it only built them after four people died at the bus stop. The numbers also undercut the standard objection that slowing cars hurts business: collisions and injuries fell while sales-tax revenue rose.

top_stories.source_headline: SFPD promised transparency on rape kits. It waited 10 years
top_stories.one_line: The Police Commission ordered public reporting on every rape kit in 2016, SFPD never complied, and the ten-year lapse surfaced only when The Standard requested the records this year.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: A reform the commission believed it had won a decade earlier simply was not done, and no oversight body noticed for ten years. It fit the city's pattern of issuing policing directives and then leaving compliance unchecked until an outsider asks.

top_stories.source_headline: Civil Grand Jury concludes San Francisco lacks clear emergency alert strategy
top_stories.one_line: A civil grand jury faulted San Francisco for leaving its 119-siren warning network offline since December 2019, unresolved through two mayors with no replacement plan.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: The story was not a broken siren but five and a half years of governance drift on the city's only mass-notification system, in a city sitting on the Hayward and San Andreas faults and now leaning on opt-in text alerts that reach only residents who signed up.

top_stories.source_headline: S.F. high-tech police surveillance center gets $3M gift, partly for 'counter drone' tech
top_stories.one_line: Salesforce and Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen are each giving $3 million to expand SFPD's Real Time Investigations Center, including undefined counter-drone tech, with the Board of Supervisors holding final say.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: The pattern worth naming was that the city's fastest-growing surveillance program is being built with private checks rather than public budget, routing the expansion around the appropriations fight and the 2019 oversight ordinance meant to force public debate before the city acquires exactly this kind of capability.

top_stories.source_headline: Dolores Huerta's endorsement of Scott Wiener surprises Connie Chan's allies
top_stories.one_line: Labor icon Dolores Huerta endorsed Scott Wiener over Connie Chan, who has built her congressional campaign on labor unity and lists 40 union logos.
top_stories.why_it_mattered: Huerta's pick was a symbolic defection from the labor identity Chan has made central, splitting the movement's iconography from its institutional muscle and turning the endorsement race into a contest of its own.

pattern_of_the_week.title: Cameras fast, safeguards slow
pattern_of_the_week.note: San Francisco funds watching faster than it funds the safeguards it already promised. The clearest case this week was the Real Time Investigations Center, where Salesforce and Chris Larsen fast-tracked $6 million in private gifts, part of it for counter-drone tech no one will describe, routing the expansion around the normal budget fight. Set that speed against what the city owes the public and has not delivered. The Police Commission ordered public reporting on every rape kit in 2016, and ten years later no one had noticed it was never done, until a reporter asked. The 119-siren earthquake warning network has sat dark since December 2019, into its sixth year, with no funded replacement in a city straddling two faults. Even the week's good news carried the same tell: the West Portal redesign cut collisions 60 percent, real proof the fixes work, but the city built them only after a crash killed a family of four. Two of the week's own editor notes drew the contrast without prompting, pointing from the rape-kit lapse and the silent sirens to the surveillance money moving the other way. The through-line is not that cameras are bad or that donors are villains. It is a question of sequence and who sets it. Private checks buy speed and steer the city toward capabilities the public never voted to prioritize, while the reporting, the sirens, and the street redesigns that protect people wait for a death or an outsider to force them onto the calendar.
